claims.text: What the image looks like Bone scan: multiple 'hot spots' = metastases (prostate, breast, lung)
claims.quote: Bone scan Multiple 'hot spots' = metastases (prostate, breast, lung)

claims.text: Metastases should be suspected with multiple lesions on bone scan or PET scan; with known cancer and a single bone lesion, the lesion may not be a metastasis (particularly with a low-grade cancer history and/or a long disease-free interval), so biopsy is recommended in those instances
claims.quote: Metastases should be suspected in patients who have multiple lesions on bone scan or PET scan. Although metastases are suspected in patients with known cancer and a single bone lesion, the lesion may not be a metastasis, particularly if the patient's cancer history was low-grade and/or if there has been a long disease-free interval. Thus, a biopsy of the lesion is recommended in those instances to confirm the diagnosis of a metastasis.

claims.text: Prostate cancer is most often blastic, lung cancer is most often lytic, and breast cancer may be blastic or lytic
claims.quote: Prostate cancer is most often blastic, lung cancer is most often lytic, and breast cancer may be blastic or lytic.

claims.text: Example pelvis radiograph: a lytic, destructive lesion at and above the right acetabulum, consistent with a metastasis
claims.quote: This radiograph of the pelvis shows a lytic, destructive lesion at and above the right acetabulum (arrows), consistent with a metastasis.

claims.text: Example spine radiograph: a destructive lesion affecting the upper part of the L1 vertebra (note the missing pedicle)
claims.quote: This metastasis is visible on plain radiographs as a destructive lesion affecting the upper part of the L1 vertebra (note the missing pedicle).

claims.text: Example femur image: bone destruction in the proximal femur from a renal cell carcinoma metastasis; its location and extent make the risk of fracture extremely high (impending fracture)
claims.quote: This image shows bone destruction due to a metastasis secondary to renal cell carcinoma in the proximal femur. The location and extent of bone destruction make the risk of fracture extremely high (impending fracture).
claims.locator: Lytic Metastasis in the Proximal Femur image caption

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Next step (her chart): bone pain + known cancer → bone scan first; MRI for cord compression risk
claims.quote: Bone pain + known cancer → bone scan first; MRI for cord compression risk

claims.text: If metastases are suspected, a radionuclide whole-body scan or PET/CT is usually done: more sensitive than radiographs for early and asymptomatic bone metastases, and it can scan the entire body; lesions are usually presumed to be metastases if the patient has a known primary cancer
claims.quote: If metastases are suspected, a radionuclide whole-body scan or PET/CT is usually done. Bone scan or PET/CT is more sensitive for early and asymptomatic bone metastases than radiographs and can be used to scan the entire body. Lesions on the scan are usually presumed to be metastases if the patient has a known primary cancer.

claims.text: Workup of unknown origin: history, physical examination and labs (complete blood count, metabolic panel, serum/urine protein electrophoresis, prostate-specific antigen in men); radiograph of the entire bone; CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis; whole-body technetium-99m bone scanning to identify other sites; biopsy to confirm origin of the primary tumor
claims.quote: History, physical examination, and laboratory testing (complete blood count, metabolic panel, serum/urine protein electrophoresis, prostate-specific antigen in men) Radiograph of the entire bone Advanced imaging (CT scan of the chest/abdomen/pelvis) Whole-body radionuclide technecium-99m bone scanning to identify other sites of metastases Biopsy to confirm origin of the primary tumor

claims.text: Considered in all patients over 40 years old with unexplained bone pain, particularly with a known cancer history, pain or radiographic abnormalities at more than one site, or imaging findings that suggest metastases to other locations
claims.quote: Metastatic bone tumors are considered in all patients over 40 years old with unexplained bone pain, but particularly in patients who have A known cancer history Pain or radiographic abnormalities at more than one site Findings on imaging studies that suggest metastases to other locations

claims.text: Known solid organ cancer with a new destructive bone lesion may require a biopsy to confirm metastatic disease and exclude a second primary tumor
claims.quote: Patients with known solid organ cancer and a new destructive bone lesion may require a biopsy to confirm metastatic disease and exclude a second primary tumor.

claims.text: Causes Any cancer can metastasize to bone, but carcinomas are the most common, particularly from breast, lung, prostate, kidney, thyroid and colon
claims.quote: Any cancer has the potential to metastasize to bone, but metastases from carcinomas are the most common, particularly those arising in the following solid organs: Breast Lung Prostate Kidney Thyroid Colon

claims.text: Breast cancer is the most common cancer to metastasize to bone; any bone may be involved; spread below the mid forearm or mid calf (acral metastasis) is uncommon and results most often from lung or renal cancer
claims.quote: Breast cancer is the most common cancer to metastasize to bone. Any bone may be involved with metastases. Metastatic disease does not commonly spread to bone below the mid forearm or mid calf, but when it occurs in those sites (acral metastasis), it results most often from lung or renal cancer.

claims.text: Symptoms Bone pain, although metastases may remain asymptomatic for some time; they may cause symptoms before the primary tumor is suspected or appear in patients with a known cancer
claims.quote: Metastases manifest as bone pain, although they may remain asymptomatic for some time. Bone metastases may cause symptoms before the primary tumor is suspected or may appear in patients with a known diagnosis of cancer.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Usually radiation therapy for symptomatic, large or progressively enlarging lesions; surgery to stabilize bone at risk of pathologic fracture or resect highly diseased bone (with joint reconstruction if needed); kyphoplasty or vertebroplasty for certain painful vertebral fractures
claims.quote: Usually radiation therapy for symptomatic or large or progressively enlarging lesions Surgery to stabilize bone at risk of pathologic fracture or resect highly diseased bone (with joint reconstruction if needed) Kyphoplasty or vertebraplasty for certain painful vertebral fractures

claims.text: Radiation therapy combined with selected chemotherapeutic or hormonal drugs is the most common treatment; early radiation and osteoclast inhibitors (bisphosphonates [eg, zoledronate] or denosumab) slow bone destruction; some tumors are more likely to heal after radiation (eg, breast, prostate, myeloma) than others (eg, lung cancer, renal cell carcinoma)
claims.quote: Radiation therapy, combined with selected chemotherapeutic or hormonal drugs, is the most common treatment modality. Radiation therapy is used for lesions that are symptomatic and for larger lesions that, if they progress, risk leading to pain, fracture, and/or a more difficult stabilization procedure. Early use of radiation and medications that inhibit osteoclasts (bisphosphonates [eg, zoledronate] or denosumab) slow bone destruction. Some tumors are more likely to heal after radiation therapy (eg, breast, prostate, and myeloma) than others (eg, lung cancer and renal cell carcinoma).

claims.text: Pathologic fractures may require surgery to fix the fracture or replace the fractured bone segment
claims.quote: Pathologic fractures may require treatment with surgery, to fix the fracture or replace the fractured bone segment.
